opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the big realization for me was that character- and byte-level models are really appealing in principle. You get rid of the tokenizer, which has all these well-documented problems. Tokenizers are brittle to spelling variation and noise, they handle morphology awkwardly, and they're really unfair across languages. A sentence in a lower-resource language or a non-Latin script can get split into many more tokens than the equivalent English sentence. That means it costs more, it uses up more of the context window, and the model often does worse on it.

So the question I kept coming back to was: if byte-level modeling is so nice conceptually, why isn't everyone doing it? And the answer, pretty consistently, is efficiency. When you operate on raw bytes, your sequences get much longer, often four or five times longer than with subword tokens, and sometimes more for certain scripts. With attention scaling quadratically in sequence length, that becomes really expensive in both training and inference. So the tokenizer is acting as a kind of compression step, and if you remove it you pay for it in compute.

That framing pushed me toward a specific research direction. Instead of treating tokenization as a fixed preprocessing step, could we let the model learn how to compress its input? Could it figure out which bytes it actually needs to keep around and which it can merge or drop, in a way that adapts to the content? That's what led to the work on MrT5, where we took ByT5, a byte-level encoder-decoder model, and added a learned deletion mechanism. After a few encoder layers, the model decides which positions to delete, so the rest of the network runs on a much shorter sequence. We wanted that deletion to be dynamic and learned end to end, not hard-coded with heuristics.

What was exciting was that we could get substantial reductions in sequence length, and real speedups in runtime, while keeping performance pretty close to the original model on downstream tasks. We also saw that the model learned sensible behavior. It would compress more aggressively where there was redundancy, and it adapted differently across languages, which is exactly the kind of flexibility a fixed tokenizer can't give you.

More broadly, I think it shifted my view of the problem. The question isn't really tokenizers versus no tokenizers. It's: where should the compression happen, and who decides? My bet is that letting the model learn that, rather than fixing it in advance with a frequency-based algorithm, is going to be a big part of making these tokenizer-free models practical at scale.

r001.rationale: The response asks why byte-level modeling is not widely used and discusses learned compression, but it does not raise what character- or byte-level models learn about words.

r002.rationale: The response explicitly identifies efficiency as the consistent reason these models are not widely adopted, citing longer byte sequences and the resulting compute costs.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so for me it really started from this sense of frustration, honestly. Tokenization is this piece of the pipeline that everybody kind of knows is a hack, right? We have these subword tokenizers like BPE that are trained totally separately from the model, with a totally different objective, and then the model just has to live with whatever segmentation it gets. And you see the consequences all over the place: models struggle with spelling, with counting characters, with arithmetic, with morphologically rich languages, with code, with anything where the natural unit doesn't line up with what the tokenizer happened to learn. There's also this really unfortunate fairness dimension where some languages get way more tokens per word than English, so they're more expensive and often get worse quality.

So the obvious question is, why don't we just get rid of tokenization and model bytes or characters directly? And people have tried that, going back years. But the reason it hasn't taken off is pretty simple when you look at it: efficiency. If you operate at the byte level, your sequences are something like four or five times longer than they'd be with a subword tokenizer. Attention is quadratic in sequence length, so that's a big compute hit, and even beyond attention, you're spending a full transformer forward pass on every single byte. And a lot of those bytes are extremely predictable. If you've generated the first few characters of a common word, the rest is basically free information. It feels wasteful to spend the same amount of compute on that as you do on a genuinely hard decision.

When I framed it that way, the problem stopped looking like "tokenization versus no tokenization" and started looking like a compute allocation problem. Subword tokenizers are actually doing something reasonable: they're spending less compute on predictable stuff by grouping it together. The issue is that they're doing it with a frozen, heuristic method decided before training. So the direction I went in with MrT5 was, what if the model learns where to spend its compute? You start from a byte-level model, like ByT5, and you add a mechanism in the encoder that learns to delete tokens after a few layers. The model figures out which byte positions carry redundant information and merges or drops them, so the deeper layers operate on a much shorter sequence. You get a lot of the efficiency back, but the decision is learned end-to-end, it's data-dependent, and it can adapt across languages instead of baking in an English-centric vocabulary.

So the big-picture thesis that came out of that is that the problem with character and byte models was never really about modeling ability. They're perfectly capable of learning language. It was about the cost, and cost is something you can design around. Once you accept that, there's this whole space of architectures that get the benefits of operating on raw bytes without paying the full price for it, and that's really what's shaped the research since then.

r001.rationale: The response asks why not model bytes or characters directly and says these models can learn language, but it does not raise the question of what they learn about words.

r002.rationale: The response identifies efficiency as the reason byte-level models have not taken off, citing longer sequences and greater compute costs.

astra-6.text:
I started by thinking about the efficiency problem. With characters or bytes, you’re asking the model to process much longer sequences, and to spend computation figuring out patterns that a tokenizer effectively gives it for free. So a comparison with a token-level model can end up being a comparison of how efficiently you’ve allocated compute, rather than what the models can ultimately learn.

That led me toward a more basic question: how much of the structure we build into language models is actually necessary, and how much is just a useful shortcut? Instead of assuming that words or subwords are the right units, I became interested in how models learn structure from the input, and what kinds of inductive biases help them do that. Character- and byte-level modeling was a way into that broader question about learning and representation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the question for me was: why are we so committed to tokens? Working at the character or byte level is appealing because you don’t have to build in a particular vocabulary. But then your sequences get much longer, and the model has to spend computation figuring out how those smaller units fit together before it can do the higher-level work.

So I started thinking about whether that was a fundamental limitation or a consequence of the architectures we use. Could we let the model learn how to group the input into useful units, rather than making that decision ahead of time with a tokenizer? That pushed my research toward learning that structure within the model—trying to preserve the flexibility of byte-level input while making the computation more efficient.
